query: Which material can be used for enhance glass-forming ability, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Incorporating a minor amount of boron into a Zr-based alloy will enhance its glass-forming ability by promoting atomic size mismatch and local packing frustration, which suppresses crystallization.
generation.material_initial_state: Zr-based metallic alloy in its standard composition with known crystallization tendencies.
generation.intervention: Alloying with a small concentration (e.g., 1-5 atomic percent) of boron.
generation.conditions: Samples prepared under identical melting and cooling conditions in an inert atmosphere.
generation.structural_mediator: Boron atoms, due to their small atomic size relative to Zr, disrupt the periodicity of the alloy, increasing the complexity of atomic arrangements.
generation.mechanism: The addition of boron leads to increased atomic size mismatches and enhances topological and chemical disorder, which in turn delays nucleation and growth of crystalline phases, thereby stabilizing the supercooled liquid state.
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified alloy with boron will exhibit a broader supercooled liquid region and a higher glass transition temperature compared to the unmodified alloy, indicating enhanced glass-forming ability.
generation.baseline: The unmodified Zr-based alloy under the same processing conditions.
generation.boundary: The enhancement is expected only in the specified boron concentration range and for systems where the atomic size mismatch is significant; effects may differ in other alloy systems or at much higher boron concentrations.
generation.uncertainty: While the general mechanism of size mismatch enhancing glass formation is supported by existing ideas in metallic glasses, the optimal boron concentration and its precise quantitative effect on the glass transition and crystallization kinetics remain to be verified experimentally.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Zr-based alloy samples: one set with a 1-5 atomic percent addition of boron and a control set without boron. Both sets should be cast under identical cooling rates using a rapid quenching technique. Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) will be used to measure the glass transition temperature (Tg), crystallization onset temperature, and width of the supercooled liquid region.
measurements: DSC thermograms comparing Tg and crystallization exotherms
X-ray diffraction patterns to confirm amorphous structure
Microstructural analysis to detect any crystalline phases
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the boron-alloyed samples do not show a statistically significant increase in the supercooled liquid region width or higher Tg compared to the control samples, or if crystallization is not delayed despite the addition of boron, then the hypothesis that boron enhances glass-forming ability in this system is refuted.
